en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Twenty, Chapter on Mātaṅga.
8. The Bhallātiya Jātaka:
There was a king named Bhallātiya;
abandoning his kingdom, he went out hunting.
He arrived at Gandhamādana, the best of mountains,
which was in full bloom and frequented by kinnaras;
having restrained the host of Sālūra, he—
Having laid aside his bow and quiver,
he approached, desiring to speak words to where the kinnaras were standing.
“On the slopes of the Himalayas, on the bank of the Hema river,
why do you stand here and constantly deliberate?
I ask you, you who possess the form of human bodies.”
"How do people in the world of men know you?
"We roam along the Sītodakā River, past the pale, three-peaked Malla mountain."
“Deer with human-like radiance and color—
do you not know us to be *kimpurisas*, hunter?
“You wail in a most pitiable manner.”
And you were embraced by your beloved, though she was dear to you.
I ask you, who possess the form of human bodies:
why do you weep here in the forest, so devoid of joy?
You lament over a form so difficult to find,
though you were embraced by one dear to you;
I ask you, O you who possess the beauty of human bodies:
Why do you lament here in the forest, lacking confidence?
Why do you wail in such a piteous manner?
For you were embraced by your beloved.
“I ask you, who possess the form of human bodies:
why do you grieve here in the forest, lacking confidence?
“We have stayed overnight apart from us, O hunter.”
"Reluctantly remembering one another,
we grieve as we reflect upon that single night,
thinking: 'That night shall never come again.'"
“That regret which one feels for even a single night—
like wealth lost or a father deceased—
I ask you, O you who possess the form of human bodies:”
“How did he make his dwelling without a residence?
“This river that you see here, with its swift current,
its various trees for cover, and its rocky banks;”
"He is dear to me, especially in the rainy season;
he follows after me, as I think.
And so, I plucked the *aṅkolaka* flowers.
Atimuttaka and Sattaliyothika:
"He will be dear to me as he wears his garland, and I too,
wearing my garland, shall approach him."
I myself shall gather these kuravaka flowers,
uddālaka, pāṭali, and sindhuvāraka;
"He will be dear to me, wearing this garland."
And I would approach that Mālinī.
And I would gather the blossoms of the well-flowered Sāla tree and make a garland.
‘He will be dear to me, wearing his garland,
and I, wearing my garland, will approach him. And I,
[near] a well-flowered *sāla* tree—
I shall gather flowers and make a bed;
this will serve as our bedding where we shall dwell for the night.
And I, being heedless, ground agarwood and sandalwood upon a stone, thinking:
"He will be dear to me with his limbs anointed."
"And I, having provoked him, would have approached him.
Then there came a swift-flowing torrent of water,
pushing aside the *sāla*, *salaḷa*, and *kaṇṇikāra* trees.
In that brief moment,
the river became very difficult for me to cross;
we were then standing on both banks.
Beholding one another,
we both wept at times and laughed at times;
that night came upon us with great difficulty.
Early in the morning, when the sun had risen,
O hunter, having crossed the river at the four-way junction,
we both embraced one another.
Sometimes we weep, sometimes we laugh.
O hunter, seven hundred and three times have we lived here in this place before.
“O protector of the earth, this life is so brief;
who here would dwell apart from their beloved?
And how long, my dear friend, is the lifespan of you all?”
If you know his lifespan, speak it!
Whether it be from tradition or from having come down through the elders,
declare that to me without wavering.
“Ludda, our lifespan is a thousand years,
and there is no evil disease to interrupt it;
suffering is slight and happiness is abundant.”
“Without having abandoned passion, we shall give up our lives.
Having heard this from the non-humans, [he thought:
“Bhallātiya’s life is now at its end.”
He turned back and did not go hunting;
he gave gifts and enjoyed his wealth.
Having heard this from the non-human beings, [he acted accordingly].
Greet one another and do not quarrel;
let not the transgression of your own deeds burn you,
as it did for those Kimpurisas for a single night.
Having heard this from the non-humans:
"Be in harmony, do not engage in dispute;
let there be no remorse for you on account of the transgression of your own actions."
"Just as you have for a single night with that kinnara.
"With a joyful mind, I hear your various words,
which are full of meaning and beneficial."
"Releasing your voice, you dispel my fear;
O ascetic who brings happiness, let me live for a long time.
The Eighth Bhallātiya Jātaka.
